newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt market calm but stable amid Zaire turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt market calm but stable amid Zaire turmoil.

text.p: The price of cobalt is failing to seriously react to the chaos in war-torn Zaire, one of the world's leading producers of the strategic metal, European traders commented on Monday.
Over the weekend rebel sources said they were aiming to overthrow the capital city of Kinshasa and the southern mining town of Lubumbashi which lies in the heart of the mineral rich region of Shaba.
The announcement followed the fall of Zaire's third city Kisangani.
European traders said the impact of the fighting in Zaire was a stabilising factor in the cobalt market which showed signs of recovering from recent downside pressure.

However, the recent firming in prices of the metal used in super-alloys, batteries and industrial magnets was said to be largely due to a turn around in market sentiment as operators eyed supply/demand data.
The state owned mining company Gecamines produced around 5,000 of cobalt in 1996, a source close to the company said at a recent minor metals seminar in Miami.
The source said supply lines to the plant and routes for shipments were still operating.
Even if the rebels captured the mines and production plant, output would only be stopped temporarily at most because it was an important hard currency earner, the source added.
One European trader said that production was still flowing. "I have heard nothing to counter this view so far."
Others generally believed production was still running but were quick to dismiss the recent comments from the source close to Gecamines.
"I cannot believe production of cobalt will remain unaffected if there is any conflict near the mines, trader said.
But whatever the outcome of the Zairean conflict most European traders polled by Reuters agreed prices had the potential to climb over the coming months.
The metal is extensively used in the aircraft industry and at present it is impossible to produce a jet engine without the use of cobalt alloys.
"The production of passenger aircraft is booming and likely to do so over the next few years," one trader said.
At the start of 1997 Moody's Investors Service said in its annual report that overall the anticipated recovery in the commercial aircraft industry and general aviation sectors is well underway.
Further evidence of demand for cobalt emerged at the recent meeting in Miami.
Increase in the use of lithium-ion batteries in personal computers and other applications will sharply increase the demand for cobalt in Japan.
On the other side of the coin traders argued that production of all forms of cobalt was set to grow in 1997.
"New sources of production are likely to be seen while existing facilities are set to up output," one trader said.
Referring to the above scenario the trader believed that supply would roughly match the expected growth in demand.
"The market is set to remain well balanced," the trader said.
On Monday high grade cobalt was indicated at around $21/$22 a pound, against a recent $19/20.
Lower graded Russian material was at $19/$20, against $17/$18.
Zaire also is a producer of copper, though annual production is very low at around 40,000 tonnes.
Traders said current copper production is a drop in the ocean compared to the 500,000 tonnes output of contained metal it produced in the early 1980s.
On Monday three months delivery copper was indicated at around $2,355/59, little changed from Friday's London Metal Exchange afternoon close.
